1009.title: Gardens with running water
1009.hook: four-part gardens with water channels, reflecting the gardens of the Qur'an
1009.howItsDone: Visitors still walk the channel gardens of places such as the Alhambra's Generalife, Isfahan and the Taj Mahal, and some Muslim homes keep courtyard gardens with a fountain or pool at the center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dome and the minaret: a sky you can stand under, and a tower for the call. Your line was: sky and voice. When did you look up on purpose? Day one thousand nine.

"Gardens underneath which rivers flow." That's a phrase from the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, describing what waits for those who believe and do good. Now step through a gate into a walled courtyard in Isfahan, or Granada, or Agra. Stone paths cross in the middle. Along each path runs a narrow channel of water, so shallow it barely moves, holding a strip of sky. Where the channels meet, there's a pool, or a fountain murmuring. Trees, shade, the smell of wet stone. A garden, with water running beside every path. Today: gardens with running water.
screen: `GARDENS UNDERNEATH WHICH RIVERS FLOW.` → `A WALLED COURTYARD.` → `CHANNELS MEET AT A POOL.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an's word for paradise, jannah, is the ordinary Arabic word for a garden. So when the Qur'an describes the life to come, it describes shade, fruit and water. One passage, in surah forty-seven, even names its rivers: rivers of water that never goes stale, rivers of milk, rivers of wine, rivers of honey. Garden builders worked with a plan that is often called by a Persian name, chahar bagh, four gardens: a walled rectangle split by water channels into four parts that meet at a center. Some readers link those channels to the rivers of surah forty-seven. Others point out that walled Persian gardens are older than Islam, and say Muslims took up the old plan and gave it new meaning. Both can be true. Either way, consider what water meant to the people who built these. Isfahan, Agra and Granada are hot in summer. Water you could hear was wealth. Water you could see moving was life. A garden with running water was a small earthly reminder of a promise, built by hand, to be walked in. And these gardens were made for sitting. Not for racing through: for sitting beside a channel in the shade and listening. Some were planted around tombs, so that the dead rested inside a picture of the garden they hoped for. In the Qur'an the garden is a promise. The garden on earth was a way of keeping that promise in view. Under which rivers flow.
screen: `JANNAH: A GARDEN.` · `RIVERS OF WATER, MILK, WINE, HONEY.` · `FOUR GARDENS, OLDER ROOTS.` · `MADE FOR SITTING.` · then, large: `UNDER WHICH RIVERS FLOW.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit near water or a plant. A fountain, a glass of water on the table, a tap running gently into a bowl, a houseplant, a tree outside the window. Settle, and breathe. Look at it as if it were the center of a garden, the place where all the paths meet. If it's water, listen to it, or watch the light on it. If it's a plant, choose one leaf: its edge, its color, the way it's turned toward the light. If you pray, you can say al-hamdu lillah, praise be to God, for water. If you don't, just stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Jannah. The Qur'an's word for paradise and garden, pictured as gardens under which rivers flow, and echoed in walled courtyards split by channels. Today's word.
Your line: under which rivers flow. Today, drink one glass of water slowly, and think about what it took to reach you. Day one thousand nine.

1010.title: Carpets and tiles
1010.hook: prayer rugs, Persian carpets, Iznik tiles
1010.howItsDone: At home or at work, a Muslim may pray on a prayer rug laid toward Mecca, though any clean place is enough; mosque floors are commonly carpeted, and some Ottoman mosques are lined with Iznik tiles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gardens with running water, and the jannah they point toward. Your line was: under which rivers flow. Did you drink a glass of water slowly? Day one thousand ten.

At prayer time, in the corner of an office, someone unrolls a small rectangle of cloth, smooths a wrinkle with one hand, checks the direction, and steps onto it. A minute ago this was the spot by the printer. Now it's a place of prayer. Far away, in an old mosque in Istanbul, the walls are covered in tiles: deep blue, turquoise, and a red like a ripe tomato, painted with tulips and carnations. Underfoot, a carpet. On the walls, a garden in glazed clay. Cloth and clay. Today: carpets and tiles.
screen: `A RUG UNROLLED BY THE PRINTER.` → `A MOSQUE WALL OF TILES.` → `CLOTH AND CLAY.`

segments.voice: Start with the rug. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says the earth has been made for him a place of prayer, and pure. Any clean ground will do. So a prayer rug isn't required. It does a quieter job: it marks off a clean patch of floor, and it lets someone carry a place of prayer rolled up under one arm. Another hadith in al-Bukhari mentions the Prophet praying on a small mat. On many prayer rugs, the weaver puts an arch at one end, the shape of the mihrab, the niche in a mosque wall that shows the direction of prayer. Lay the rug the right way, and the little arch points where to face. Then there are the great carpets, Persian and Turkish and more, knotted by hand. Some are woven as gardens, yesterday's channels and all: a garden you can keep on the floor. The Qur'an's own picture of paradise has carpets in it. In Pickthall's translation: "And silken carpets spread." Now the tiles. In the town of Iznik, in Turkey, potters made tiles in white, cobalt blue and turquoise, with a red that sits up slightly from the glaze. The Ottomans lined mosques with them, so tulips climb the walls around the people praying. One more thing, because it gets told a lot: people say weavers leave a deliberate mistake in every carpet, because only God is perfect. It's a story people tell. There's no sure source behind it, and a weaver's mistakes can arrive on their own. Woven prayer.
screen: `ANY CLEAN GROUND WILL DO.` · `AN ARCH THAT POINTS THE WAY.` · `A GARDEN ON THE FLOOR.` · `TULIPS CLIMB THE IZNIK TILES.` · then, large: `WOVEN PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The practice: touch a woven thing. A rug, a scarf, a blanket, the sleeve of what you're wearing. Settle, and breathe. Run your fingers slowly across it. Feel where the threads cross, and cross again. Someone put every one of those crossings there, by hand or with a machine that someone built and tended. Think about those hands for a moment. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If you don't, just thank them, quietly, wherever they are. The bell holds the time.
Carpets and tiles. The prayer rug that marks off clean ground, and the glazed tiles that turned mosque walls into gardens. Today's word.
Your line: woven prayer. Today, notice one handmade thing you use, and handle it with a little more care. Day one thousand ten.

1011.title: The Burdah
1011.hook: al-Busiri's poem of the cloak, praising the Prophet ﷺ, sung across the world
1011.howItsDone: In Egypt, Turkey, North and East Africa and South and Southeast Asia, groups gather to sing the Burdah, often around the Prophet's birthday; other Muslims, following reformist scholars, do not recite it or object to some of its lines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, carpets and tiles: a rug with a little arch, and tulips climbing a mosque wall. Your line was: woven prayer. What handmade thing did you handle with care? Day one thousand eleven.

A poet lies in bed in Egypt, half his body unable to move. That's how the story begins, the one people tell about Sharaf al-Din al-Busiri. With nothing left to him but words, he composes a long poem in praise of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and recites it, weeping, over and over. One night he dreams that the Prophet is standing beside him. In the dream, the Prophet passes his hand over him and lays his cloak, his burdah, across his body. In the morning, the story says, al-Busiri gets up and walks out of the house. Today: the Burdah.
screen: `A POET WHO CANNOT MOVE.` → `A DREAM, AND A CLOAK.` → `IN THE MORNING, HE WALKS.`

segments.voice: Whether someone hears that healing as a miracle, a blessing or a story, the poem itself is real, and it traveled. Its formal title is long; people simply call it the Burdah, the poem of the cloak. It opens the old way Arabic poems opened, with longing: a lover remembering a place and a neighbor, unable to stop his tears. Then it turns. The poet confesses his own faults and warns his soul against its appetites. And then he pours out praise: the Prophet's birth, his night journey, his patience, his mercy. Every line ends on the same rhyme, the letter mim, so the whole poem rings like one long bell. Then people sang it. Across Egypt, Turkey, North and East Africa, South and Southeast Asia, groups gather to sing it together, often with a refrain between the verses, often around the Prophet's birthday. Why praise the Prophet in poetry at all? Those who love the Burdah point to a verse of the Qur'an. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." A poem like this is one way of answering that. Not every Muslim sings it. Some scholars, especially in reform movements, have objected to a few of its lines, saying they ask of the Prophet what only God can give. Those who love the poem read the same lines as asking for his intercession, which they believe God grants. Both sides would say they are guarding the Prophet's honor. And the poem keeps being sung. The poem of the cloak.
screen: `A POEM NAMED FOR A CLOAK.` · `LONGING, CONFESSION, PRAISE.` · `ONE RHYME, LIKE A BELL.` · `SUNG, AND ARGUED OVER.` · then, large: `THE POEM OF THE CLOAK.`

segments.voice: The practice: listen to it sung. If you can, find a recording of the Burdah and play the opening for the length of the sit. If you can't right now, sit with the sound of a single rhyme instead: a soft hum, mmm, on every out-breath. Settle, and breathe. There's no need to follow the Arabic. Listen to how the voices repeat, and how the refrain comes back around. If you pray, you can send blessings on the Prophet with the words Muslims use: sallallahu alayhi wa sallam. If you don't, simply listen to people praising someone they love. The bell holds the time.
The Burdah. Al-Busiri's poem of the cloak, praising the Prophet, every line rhymed on one letter, sung in many lands. Today's word.
Your line: the poem of the cloak. Today, say out loud one specific thing you admire in someone you love, and say it to them. Day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: The voice
1012.hook: the adhan and Qur'an recited in maqams, melodic modes
1012.howItsDone: Muslims learn tajwid from teachers, often in mosque classes, and listen to celebrated reciters; muezzins in different cities call the same words of the adhan in their own local melodies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Burdah, al-Busiri's poem rhymed on a single letter. Your line was: the poem of the cloak. Whom did you praise out loud? Day one thousand twelve.

Two recordings of the same call to prayer. In the first, the muezzin's voice rises slowly, leans on one note, falls, and rises again, with something like an ache in it. In the second, the voice is brighter and quicker, climbing in little steps. The words are the same in both, line for line. The tune is not. Neither melody is written down as sheet music. They live in the throat, passed from teacher to student. Today, the last stop among the arts: the voice.
screen: `TWO RECORDINGS, ONE CALL.` → `SAME WORDS, DIFFERENT TUNES.` → `IT LIVES IN THE THROAT.`

segments.voice: We've walked through calligraphy, geometry, the vine, the dome, the garden, the carpet and the poem. The arts end where a Muslim day begins: with a voice. The Qur'an asks to be recited. In Pickthall's translation, the Prophet is told to "chant the Qur'an in measure." And a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, tells people to beautify the Qur'an with their voices. So there are rules, called tajwid: how long to hold a vowel, which letters press against each other, where to stop and where never to stop. Tajwid governs the sounds. It doesn't fix the melody. Into that space come the maqamat, the melodic modes of Arab music, with names like bayati, hijaz, rast and saba. Each has its own color; some listeners hear saba as sorrowful and hijaz as reaching. A skilled reciter may move from one mode to another as the meaning of the verses shifts, from warning to mercy, from story to promise. Here Muslims differ, and fairly. Some scholars warn against reciting by musical rules, afraid that the tune will start to bend the words. Others welcome the modes, as long as tajwid comes first. Both sides would say the words lead and the voice serves. The call to prayer works the same way: fixed words, and melodies that change from Cairo to Istanbul to Jakarta. No instrument. No score. Only a human voice, trained and offered to God. The voice is the art.
screen: `CHANT THE QUR'AN IN MEASURE.` · `TAJWID: THE RULES OF SOUND.` · `MAQAMS: COLORS OF MELODY.` · `THE WORDS LEAD, THE VOICE SERVES.` · then, large: `THE VOICE IS THE ART.`

segments.voice: The practice: listen to two adhans. Find two recordings from different places and play a minute of each, or one now and one later today. Settle, and breathe. Don't follow the words. Follow the shape: where the voice rises, where it holds, where it falls. If you can't play them now, listen to the room around you instead, and to your own breath. If you pray, you can answer the call quietly, repeating its words after the muezzin. If you don't, just listen. The bell holds the time.
The voice. The Qur'an and the call to prayer, sung with no instrument, shaped by the rules of tajwid and colored by melodic modes. Today's word.
Your line: the voice is the art. Today, read one thing aloud, slowly, and let your voice care about the words. Day one thousand twelve.

1013.title: The endowment
1013.hook: a property given forever for good: a well, a school, a hospital
1013.howItsDone: Muslims still found waqfs for mosques, schools, wells and scholarships, often through charities that manage the endowment and spend only its income, and speak of it as sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the voice: the Qur'an and the call to prayer, sung with no instrument. Your line was: the voice is the art. What did you read aloud? Day one thousand thirteen.

Umar ibn al-Khattab had come into a piece of land at Khaybar, and, as he put it, he had never owned anything he valued more. He went to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asked what to do with it. The answer, reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, comes to this: if you wish, keep the land itself, and give away what it produces. So Umar did. The land could not be sold, or given away, or inherited. Its harvest went to the poor, to relatives, to freeing slaves, to the cause of God, to travelers and to guests. Keep the root. Give the fruit. A new part of the path begins: institutions. Today: the endowment.
screen: `UMAR'S LAND AT KHAYBAR.` → `KEEP THE ROOT, GIVE THE FRUIT.` → `A NEW PART: INSTITUTIONS.`

segments.voice: The word is waqf: property set aside so it can never be sold, with its income given for good, on and on. You've already met waqf at work on this path, quietly paying for things: the hospitals that sent no bill, the colleges where students got a room and bread. Here's the idea underneath. A gift usually ends. You give a meal, and it's eaten. A waqf is built not to end. A row of shops is endowed, and their rent pays a teacher. A farm is endowed, and its grain feeds the hungry. The giver dies. The shops are still rented. The teacher is still paid. Why give this way? A saying of the Prophet in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that brings benefit, and a righteous child who prays for them. Ongoing charity, sadaqah jariyah, charity that keeps flowing. A waqf is that hadith set in stone and soil. And the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love." Umar gave the land he valued most. Sultans endowed mosques and hospitals. Ordinary people, women and men, endowed a fountain, a shelf of books, a bed in a hospital. Some waqfs fed people long after their founders died. Others were mismanaged, seized, or simply forgotten; forever is a hard promise for human hands to keep. Today some Muslims are reviving the idea, with endowed wells, scholarships and funds. Given forever.
screen: `A GIFT BUILT NOT TO END.` · `THE RENT PAYS THE TEACHER.` · `THREE THINGS OUTLAST A LIFE.` · `SPEND OF THAT WHICH YE LOVE.` · then, large: `GIVEN FOREVER.`

segments.voice: The practice: support a lasting cause. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something good you'd like to still be running after you're gone: a library, a scholarship, a clean-water project, a mosque, a hospital, a habit you teach a child. Choose one. Then choose the smallest real step toward it: a small recurring gift, a skill you could teach, a name to look up later. If you pray, you can ask that it outlast you. If you don't, simply settle on the step. The bell holds the time.
Waqf. Property set aside forever, never to be sold, with its income given for good. Today's word.
Your line: given forever. Today, give one thing that keeps giving: teach a skill, set up something recurring, or plant something that will outgrow you. Day one thousand thirteen.

1014.title: The school
1014.hook: the madrasah teaching Qur'an, law, language and more
1014.howItsDone: Muslim children and adults study in mosque circles and madrasahs of every kind, from weekend Qur'an classes to seminaries; in traditional study a student may still receive an ijazah from a teacher, naming the chain of teachers behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, waqf, the endowment: keep the root, give the fruit. Your line was: given forever. What did you give that keeps on giving? Day one thousand fourteen.

A pillar in a big mosque. A teacher sits with his back against it, a book open on his knees. Around him on the floor, in a half circle, his students: a boy from the town, an old merchant, a traveler who arrived last week. He reads a line, explains it, and they write. When the lesson ends, they stand up and the circle disappears. Tomorrow it forms again at the same pillar. That circle is called a halaqa, and learning in Muslim lands often happened in circles like it, before there was any building called a school. Today: the school.
screen: `A TEACHER AGAINST A PILLAR.` → `A HALF CIRCLE ON THE FLOOR.` → `THE HALAQA.`

segments.voice: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih Muslim, makes a promise: whoever travels a road seeking knowledge, God makes easy for them a road to paradise. So people traveled, and sat in circles. Over time the circles needed rooms, food, books and paid teachers, and the madrasah grew around them. You met the great colleges of Baghdad and Fez earlier on this path. Today, step inside an ordinary one. A courtyard with a fountain. Small rooms around it where students lived. A prayer hall. A shelf of books. Classes in Qur'an and hadith, law, and Arabic grammar, and in some, logic or arithmetic. And at the end, no diploma from the building. Instead, a person. You met the calligrapher's license a few days ago; the schools had their own: a teacher could give you an ijazah, written permission to teach a book, naming who had taught it to him, and who had taught that teacher, back through a chain of names. The knowledge belonged to the chain, not to the walls. One more surprise: in Arabic, madrasah simply means school. Any school. A child in Cairo goes to a madrasah to learn math and science. Places to learn.
screen: `A CIRCLE AT A PILLAR.` · `A ROAD TO KNOWLEDGE.` · `A COURTYARD OF STUDENTS.` · `THE IJAZAH: A CHAIN OF TEACHERS.` · then, large: `PLACES TO LEARN.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a school. Settle, and breathe. Bring back one place where you learned something that stayed: a classroom, a mosque circle, a library, a kitchen table, a workshop. Then one teacher there. What did they hand you that you still carry? If you pray, you can pray for them, living or gone. If you don't, simply hold their face in mind for a moment. Later today, if you can, write a thank-you: to the person, or to the school itself. The bell holds the time.
The school. From the halaqa at a mosque pillar to the madrasah with its courtyard, its students and its chain of teachers. Today's word.
Your line: places to learn. Today, thank a school or a teacher in writing, even two lines. Day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: The road houses
1015.hook: caravanserais on trade routes, where travelers stayed
1015.howItsDone: Muslim travelers shorten their prayers on journeys and may postpone a Ramadan fast; zakat and other charity can go to the wayfarer, and restored caravanserais and khans still stand in cities and along old routes in Turkey, Iran and the Arab world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the school: a circle at a pillar, a courtyard of students, a chain of teachers. Your line was: places to learn. Which teacher did you thank? Day one thousand fifteen.

A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, is startlingly honest about travel. It calls travel a piece of torment: it keeps you from your sleep, your food and your drink. So, it says, when you've finished what you went for, hurry home to your family. It would make sense to anyone who has slept on an airport floor. The old trade roads were harder: dust by day, cold at night, thieves in the hills. Along them, people built houses for exactly that torment. Earlier on this path you met the Seljuk ones in Anatolia. This time, the idea underneath them all. Today: the road houses.
screen: `TRAVEL IS A PIECE OF TORMENT.` → `HURRY HOME.` → `HOUSES ALONG THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with how the faith treats the traveler, because the stone follows from it. The Qur'an makes room for someone on the road. A person on a journey in Ramadan may leave the fast and make up the days later, it says in surah two. And prayer may be shortened. In Pickthall's translation: "And when ye go forth in the land, it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship." The verse goes on to name the fear of attack. In Sahih Muslim, someone later asks Umar why people still shorten, now that the roads are safe. Umar says he wondered the same and asked the Prophet, who called it a charity from God, to be accepted. The Qur'an also names ibn al-sabil, the son of the road, the wayfarer, among those owed a share of charity. So the law leans toward the tired. The road house leans the same way. Out on the open road it was called a caravanserai. Inside a city it was often called a khan. The pattern repeats with local accents: one great gate that could be shut at night; a courtyard open to the sky; a well or a fountain; rooms around the edge for people; stalls or arcades for the animals; often a small mosque. Inside the cities, the khan was also a warehouse and a market, where merchants from far away stored their bales and did their deals. Out on the road, it was shelter, and in some, paid for by waqf, the night cost nothing. A road house turns a stranger into a guest for a night. But the honest hadith still holds. A road house isn't home. It's a place to rest, eat, sleep, and gather strength to keep going, or to go back. Rest for the traveler.

segments.voice: The practice: help a traveler. Settle, and breathe. This week took us through gardens with running water, carpets and tiles, the poem of the cloak, the voice, the endowment, the school, and now the road. Let them pass by like a caravan. Then think of someone on the road today: a friend flying, a cousin driving through the night, a coworker far from home, a stranger asking for directions. Choose one, and decide one real help: a message, a meal, a ride, a bed, a little patience at the station. If you pray, you can ask for their safe return. If you don't, simply decide. The bell holds the time.
Caravanserai. A road house with a gate, a well and a room, so a stranger could rest as a guest. Today's word.
Your line: rest for the traveler. Today, make one person's journey a little easier, or help someone get home. Day one thousand fifteen.
